title: Natural Resources and Agriculture
syllabus: WAEC Geography, Regional Geography of Nigeria: resources; agriculture. Part A: environmental resources
NERDC-based schemes: Resources of Nigeria; Renewable and non-renewable resources; Agriculture
objectives: classify natural resources as renewable or non-renewable, with examples;
locate Nigeria's main mineral resources and explain their importance;
describe the main types of agriculture practised in Nigeria;
relate the distribution of major crops and livestock to climate and soils;
explain the problems facing agriculture and suggest solutions.
describe the environmental concerns linked to farming and mining;
intro: Natural resources are things found in nature that people use to meet their needs: land, water, forests, minerals and energy sources. Nigeria is rich in both mineral and agricultural resources, but managing them well — and spreading their benefits — is one of the country's biggest challenges.

items.title: Renewable resources
items.text: Can be replaced naturally if used carefully: soil, water, forests, fish, wildlife, solar and wind energy.

items.title: Non-renewable resources
items.text: Exist in fixed amounts and cannot be replaced once used up: crude oil, natural gas, coal, tin and other minerals.

blocks.text: Even renewable resources can be destroyed by overuse — for example forests by uncontrolled logging, fish stocks by overfishing and soil by erosion. Careful management (**conservation**) is needed so that resources remain available for future generations.

blocks.text: Commercial crude oil was first discovered at **Oloibiri** (in present-day Bayelsa State) in **1956**, and exports began in 1958. Most of Nigeria's oil and gas comes from the Niger Delta. Oil brings revenue, foreign exchange and jobs, but also problems: dependence on one commodity, price swings, pollution from spills and gas flaring, and conflict over the sharing of benefits.

items: **Subsistence farming**: farmers grow food mainly for their families, on small plots with simple tools such as hoes and cutlasses.
**Bush fallowing and shifting cultivation**: land is farmed for a few years and then left to rest (fallow) so that soil fertility can recover. Rising population has shortened fallow periods.
**Mixed farming**: crops and livestock on the same farm; animal manure fertilises the crops.
**Plantation agriculture**: large estates growing one cash crop, such as oil palm or rubber, often with processing on site.
**Pastoral nomadism**: herders, mainly in the north, move cattle, sheep and goats in search of pasture and water.
**Irrigation farming**: water from rivers and dams is used to grow crops in the dry season, especially on fadama land and in irrigation schemes in the north.
**Fishing**: in rivers, lakes such as Kainji, creeks and the sea.

blocks.text: Agriculture provides food, raw materials for industries (for example cocoa, cotton, oil palm and hides), employment for a large part of the workforce, and some export earnings. Before oil, crops such as cocoa, groundnuts and palm produce were Nigeria's main exports.

items.title: Problems
items.text: Small, scattered farms; simple tools; poor storage and processing causing post-harvest losses; poor rural roads; lack of credit; pests and diseases; soil erosion; unreliable rainfall and floods; land tenure problems; conflicts between farmers and herders.

items.title: Possible solutions
items.text: Credit schemes and cooperatives; better storage and processing; improved seeds and fertilisers through extension services; irrigation and water management; better rural roads; land reform; peaceful grazing arrangements; climate-smart farming.

items: Clearing forest and savanna for new farms causes deforestation and loss of wildlife habitat.
Overgrazing and bush burning leave the soil bare, which leads to erosion and contributes to desertification.
Too much fertiliser or pesticide can wash into rivers and harm fish and drinking water.
Shrinking pasture and water, made worse by drought, has increased competition between farmers and herders.
Mining can pollute land and water. Lead released by small-scale gold processing in Zamfara State caused a serious lead-poisoning outbreak among children in 2010.

definitions: Natural resource
A material or substance found in nature that people can use.
Renewable resource
A resource that can be replaced naturally if managed well, such as forests or water.
Non-renewable resource
A resource that exists in fixed amounts and cannot be replaced, such as crude oil.
Bush fallowing
Leaving farmland to rest for some years so that its fertility can recover.
Plantation
A large estate specialising in one cash crop, such as rubber or oil palm.
Pastoral nomadism
Moving livestock from place to place in search of pasture and water.
Gas flaring
Burning off natural gas released during oil production.
Cash crop
A crop grown mainly for sale, such as cocoa, cotton or sesame, rather than for the farmer's own food.
Irrigation
Supplying water to crops from rivers, dams, wells or canals, especially in the dry season.
Cooperative
A group of farmers who pool resources to buy inputs, obtain credit, process and market produce together.
Fadama
Low-lying flood plain land beside rivers in northern Nigeria, farmed in the dry season.

worked.title: Matching a crop to its environment
worked.problem: Explain why cocoa is grown mainly in the south-west and not in the far north of Nigeria.
steps: State the crop's needs: cocoa needs high rainfall spread through most of the year, high temperatures, shade and deep, well-drained soils.
Compare with the south-west: rainfall is high, the dry season short, and forest soils are deep — conditions suit cocoa.
Compare with the far north: rainfall is low and the dry season long and harsh, so cocoa trees cannot survive there without irrigation.

worked.title: Calculating crop yield and its change
worked.problem: A farm of 2.5 hectares produced 7.5 tonnes of maize. After using improved seed and fertiliser, the same farm produced 10 tonnes. Calculate the yield before and after, and the percentage increase.
steps: Yield = production ÷ area. Before: 7.5 ÷ 2.5 = **3 tonnes per hectare**.
worked.note: Illustrative figures for practising the method.

exam_tips: When asked to locate a mineral, name the state or town (e.g. tin — Jos Plateau; coal — Enugu; iron ore — Itakpe).
Questions on agriculture often ask for problems and solutions: give each problem a matching solution.
Link crop distribution to climate and soils, not just to a list of states.

checks.q: Give two examples each of renewable and non-renewable resources found in Nigeria.
checks.a: Renewable: forests, water, soil, fish. Non-renewable: crude oil, natural gas, coal, tin.

checks.q: Where and when was commercial crude oil first discovered in Nigeria?
checks.a: At Oloibiri, in present-day Bayelsa State, in 1956.

checks.q: Why is pastoral nomadism common in the north?
checks.a: Open grassland provides pasture, the drier climate has fewer tsetse flies, and herders move seasonally to find pasture and water.

checks.q: Why is crude oil called a non-renewable resource?
checks.a: It exists in a fixed amount that took millions of years to form; once it is extracted and used it cannot be replaced within human time.

checks.q: Give two advantages of mixed farming.
checks.a: Animal manure fertilises the crops, and crop waste can feed the animals; the farmer also has more than one source of food and income, which reduces risk.

summary: Resources are renewable (soil, water, forests, fish) or non-renewable (oil, gas, coal, tin and other minerals).
Oil and gas from the Niger Delta dominate revenue and exports; other minerals include coal (Enugu), tin (Jos), limestone, iron ore (Itakpe), bitumen, gold and lead–zinc.
Farming types include subsistence, bush fallowing, mixed, plantation, pastoral nomadism, irrigation and fishing.

Root and tree crops dominate the south, mixed grains and yams the Middle Belt, and grains, groundnuts, cotton and livestock the north. Many problems limit productivity, but each has possible solutions.

structured.q: (a) Name four mineral resources found in Nigeria and state where each is found. (b) Explain three effects of the oil industry on Nigeria.
model: (a) Crude oil and natural gas — Niger Delta; coal — Enugu; tin and columbite — Jos Plateau; iron ore — Itakpe; limestone — Ewekoro, Obajana or Nkalagu (any four with correct locations).

(b) 1. Positive: oil provides most export earnings and government revenue, used to fund development. 2. Positive: it creates jobs and supports industries such as refining and petrochemicals. 3. Negative: oil spills and gas flaring pollute farmland, creeks and air in the Niger Delta, harming fishing and farming. (Overdependence on one commodity and neglect of agriculture are also accepted.)
points: (a) 1 mark for each mineral and 1 for each correct location (8).
(b) Up to 7 marks for three effects, explained.

structured.q: (a) Describe the main features of subsistence agriculture in Nigeria. (b) Outline four problems facing agriculture and suggest a solution to each.
model: (a) Small farms, often scattered; simple tools such as hoes and cutlasses; family labour; mixed cropping of food crops; low yields; produce mainly for the family, with any surplus sold locally; bush fallowing to restore fertility.

(b) Lack of capital — credit schemes and cooperatives. Poor storage — better storage and processing facilities. Poor rural roads — road building and maintenance. Pests and diseases — extension services and improved seeds and chemicals. (Land tenure, erosion and farmer–herder conflict with suitable solutions are also accepted.)
points: (b) Up to 10 marks: problem and matching solution.

structured.q: (a) Name three mineral resources of Nigeria and state where each is found. (b) Explain two benefits and two problems of oil production to Nigeria.
model: (a) For example: crude oil and gas in the Niger Delta (Rivers, Bayelsa, Delta, Akwa Ibom); tin and columbite on the Jos Plateau; limestone at Ewekoro, Obajana or Nkalagu; iron ore at Itakpe; coal at Enugu.

(b) Benefits: 1. the main source of export earnings and government revenue; 2. jobs and raw materials for refineries, petrochemicals and power. Problems: 1. pollution from oil spills and gas flaring that damages farmland, fisheries and health in the Niger Delta; 2. dependence on one commodity, so the economy suffers when oil prices fall.
points: 1 mark for each mineral named and 1 mark for its location (up to 4 marks).
1–2 marks for each benefit and problem explained (6 marks).
